relearning.title: Read: using the periodic table
relearning.description: A short reading with the apartment-building analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can use an element's location on the periodic table to predict its structure and its properties.**

**Think of an apartment building.** The floor you live on tells how high up you are, and everyone in the same column of apartments has the same floor plan. An element's **row** tells how many energy levels (floors) its electron cloud has. Its **column** tells its floor plan: how many valence electrons it has. Elements with the same floor plan live alike, so they have similar properties.

**Periods** are the rows. The period number = the number of **energy levels** (shells). **Groups** (families) are the columns. They tell the number of **valence electrons**, the electrons in the outermost energy level. Group 1 = 1 and Group 2 = 2. Then **skip the transition metals in Groups 3–12**: Group 13 = 3, up to Group 18 = 8, **except helium**, which has 2. Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties.

**Worked example:** Sulfur is in Group 16, Period 3. Group 16 → skip Groups 3–12 → 6 valence electrons. Period 3 → 3 energy levels. Fill from the inside out: **2-8-6**.

checks.prompt: Phosphorus is in Group 15, Period 3. How many valence electrons does it have? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Skip the transition metals: Group 13 = 3, Group 14 = 4, Group 15 = 5. Using the period (3) or the whole group number (15) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Why do lithium and potassium have similar chemical properties?

options.text: They are in the same period
They are in the same group, so they have the same number of valence electrons
They have the same number of energy levels

checks.explanation: Lithium and potassium are both in Group 1, so each has 1 valence electron. Elements in the same period share the number of energy levels, not their properties. Mixing up groups and periods is the common mistake.

sections.title: Metals, families and reactivity

body.text:
**Metals, nonmetals and metalloids.** The **staircase** line splits the table. **Metals** are to the left: shiny solids, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable and ductile. **Nonmetals** are to the right (plus hydrogen): gases or dull, brittle solids, and poor conductors. **Metalloids** sit on the line (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te): solids and semi-conductors, with physical properties like metals and chemical properties like nonmetals.

**The families.** Group 1 = **alkali metals**, the most reactive metals. Hydrogen is in Group 1 because it has 1 valence electron, but it is not an alkali metal. Group 2 = **alkaline earth metals**. Groups 3–12 = **transition metals**. Group 17 = **halogens**, the most reactive nonmetals. Group 18 = **noble gases**, nonreactive because they are already chemically stable.

**Reactivity.** For metals, reactivity **increases** as you move down a group. For nonmetals, reactivity **decreases** as you move down a group.

**Worked example 2:** "I am a halogen with 4 energy levels." Halogen → Group 17. 4 energy levels → Period 4. Group 17, Period 4 is **bromine (Br)**, with 7 valence electrons.

**Worked example 3:** Which is more reactive, magnesium (Group 2, Period 3) or calcium (Group 2, Period 4)? Both are alkaline earth metals, and metals get more reactive going down a group. Calcium is lower, so **calcium is more reactive**.

**Watch out for:** mixing up groups (valence electrons) and periods (energy levels), counting Groups 3–12 when you find valence electrons, giving helium 8 valence electrons, calling hydrogen an alkali metal, putting metals on the right side, and flipping the reactivity trend for nonmetals.

checks.prompt: Identify the element: I am a noble gas with 3 energy levels. Type my name or symbol.
checks.explanation: Noble gas → Group 18. 3 energy levels → Period 3. Group 18, Period 3 is argon (Ar). Mixing up the group and the period is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Chlorine (Period 3) and bromine (Period 4) are both halogens. Which is more reactive?
checks.explanation: Halogens are nonmetals, and nonmetals get less reactive going down a group. Chlorine is higher, so it is more reactive. Using the metal trend (more reactive going down) is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Potassium is in Group 1, Period 4. Predict its number of valence electrons and energy levels, and say whether it is a metal or a nonmetal. Name the part of its location that told you each one.

relearning.title: Do: flip the families, then predict an element step by step
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a worked problem one step at a time.

cards.back: A row. The period number = the number of energy levels (shells).
A column. It tells the number of valence electrons. Skip Groups 3–12 when you count.
The electrons in the outermost energy level.
Group 1: the most reactive metals. Hydrogen is in Group 1 but is not an alkali metal.
Group 17: the most reactive nonmetals, with 7 valence electrons.
Group 18: nonreactive because they are already stable. 8 valence electrons (helium has 2).
Metals are to the left, nonmetals are to the right, and metalloids sit on the line.

checks.prompt: Which part of an element's location tells you its number of energy levels?

options.text: Its side of the staircase line

checks.explanation: The period (row) number tells the energy levels. The group (column) tells the valence electrons. Mixing up the two is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: How many valence electrons does helium have?
checks.explanation: Helium is in Group 18, but it has only 2 electrons in all, so it has 2 valence electrons. Giving it 8 like the rest of Group 18 is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: An element is a shiny solid that conducts electricity well. Where is it most likely found?

options.text: To the left of the staircase line
To the right of the staircase line

checks.explanation: Shiny solids that conduct well are metals, and metals are to the left of the staircase line. Putting metals on the right side is the common mistake.

body.problem: Calcium (Ca) is in Group 2, Period 4. Its atomic number is 20. Predict its valence electrons, energy levels, electron arrangement and properties.

steps.text: A neutral calcium atom has 20 electrons. Fill from the inside out: 2-8-8-2. The outer shell holds 2, which matches Group 2.
Calcium is far to the left of the staircase line, so it is a metal: shiny and a good conductor.
It is an alkaline earth metal (Group 2). Calcium is below magnesium, and metals get more reactive going down a group, so calcium is more reactive than magnesium.

checks.prompt: Your turn: aluminum is in Group 13, Period 3. How many valence electrons and energy levels does it have?
checks.explanation: Skip Groups 3–12, so Group 13 has 3 valence electrons. Period 3 means 3 energy levels. Counting the transition metals (13) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Your turn: identify the element. I am an alkali metal with 3 energy levels. Type my name or symbol.
checks.explanation: Alkali metal → Group 1. 3 energy levels → Period 3. Group 1, Period 3 is sodium (Na). Mixing up the group and the period is the common mistake.

relearning.title: U2.LT4 Watch: periods, groups and valence electrons

checks.prompt: What does an element's period number tell you?
checks.explanation: Periods are the rows, and the period number = the number of energy levels (floors). The group tells the valence electrons. Mixing up groups and periods is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Oxygen is in Group 16. How many valence electrons does it have? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Skip the transition metals in Groups 3–12: Group 13 = 3, so Group 16 = 6 valence electrons. Counting Groups 3–12 gives 16, the common mistake.

sections.title: Valence Electrons and the Periodic Table

checks.prompt: Helium is in Group 18. How many valence electrons does it have?
checks.explanation: Group 18 = 8 valence electrons, except helium, which has only 2. Giving helium 8 is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Aluminum is in Group 13, Period 3. Which is correct?
checks.explanation: Group 13 → skip Groups 3–12 → 3 valence electrons. Period 3 → 3 energy levels. Its arrangement is 2-8-3.
